newsitem.title: ITALY: Differences remain after Italy welfare meeting.
newsitem.headline: Differences remain after Italy welfare meeting.

text.p: A meeting of the political forces supporting Prime Minister Romano Prodi's majority ended on Tuesday with differences remaining on how to cut social spending.

During the meeting, which ended after midnight, hard-left Communist Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti held his ground that his party was against welfare spending cuts, particularly on pensions and health care.
"There are differences on the outline and there is contrast on social spending. Let's hope they can be resolved," Bertinotti told reporters after the meeting.
Participants said the meeting was not polemical and neither Bertinotti nor other political leaders issued ultimatums.
Prodi's centre-left coalition relies on Communist Refoundation for its majority in the lower house.
The meeting was called to discuss Prodi's proposed rolling three-year economic target plan.

The strategy, known as the economic and financial planning document (DPEF), will outline how the government intends to cut another 25 trillion lire ($15 billion) from the public deficit in the 1998 budget.
Italian radio said Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi told the meeting that the proposed 1998 budget would be made up of about two-thirds spending cuts and one-third new revenues.
Massimo D'Alema, leader of the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), the largest force in Prodi's coalition, told reporters after the meeting that there was "no doubt" that the DPEF will be approved.
The plan is expected to be the subject of a cabinet meeting this week, most likely on Friday.
The DPEF is a crucial part of Italy's plans for stabilising state finances and keeping alive hopes of joining European economic and monetary union by the planned 1999 start date.
